Having neglected his studies at Eton, the traditional route of an Oxbridge education was barred for Orwell, and he decided to join the Indian Civil Service upon leaving in 1921. He would later describe the years he spent in Burma as a policeman in the Indian Imperial Police as ‘the wasted years’, although they were crucial in providing him inspiration for much of his writing, as well as providing motivation to succeed as an author, as opposed to spending his life in public service. His time spent as an enforcer of Britain’s imperial rule also sparked his lifelong uneasiness with authority – a factor that played an important role in his decision to move back to England and make a career out of writing. Down and Out in Paris and London – an education in writing Although – to his family’s dismay – Orwell made clear his writing ambitions upon leaving India, it would be many years before he succeeded in breaking into the literary world. Upon returning to London he made his first attempt at chronicling the lives of the lower classes and the destitute, immersing himself in their milieu in the East End of London. In 1929, he moved to Paris where he spent a year and a half in a frenzy of writing in a variety of forms. It was during this time that his first couple of articles and essays were published, and crucially he used his acute study of daily life in Paris to draw out larger issues that plagued society; these series of observations would then later become the basis for Down and Out in Paris and London (1933), most of which he had drafted by the time he moved back to London in 1930. Returning to England, Orwell left the manuscript that would eventually be Down and Out , turning his attention instead to writing fiction, struggling to adapt his clear, journalistic prose style to novels. The novels he wrote during this time include Burmese Days and A Clergyman’s Daughter . As he would later claim, they were attempts at ‘enormous naturalistic novels with unhappy endings’, which is what he had been accustomed to reading as a boy growing up in the Edwardian era. During this time, he worked several odd jobs to stay afloat, among them positions as a teacher and a bookseller, all the time continuing to write for various publications, and working on his own projects. He eventually turned his attention back to the manuscript drafted during his time in Paris, which was at that point about life among the lower classes of France, and specifically his time working in the hospitality industry. The manuscript was rejected several times, and Orwell set to reworking it, adding sections on his time in England as well. Eventually, a new left-wing publishing firm founded by Victor Gollancz took a chance on the manuscript and published it in 1933, under the pseudonym that would be well-known to English readers within the next two decades: George Orwell. The book was received favourably and sold well for a first-time author. It was an unusual blend of genres for the time: part memoir, part fly-on-the-wall account of the English and French lower classes. Some even suggested it was part fiction, an idea which has largely been refuted, although there is a sense that Orwell manipulated the sequence and details of events to suit his purpose. His clear style of writing and interest in uncovering all aspects of society was evident in this first major work. In 1936, Victor Gollancz asked him to work on a project uniquely suited to his talents: documenting the areas of Northern England most affected by the Depression. He immersed himself in the life of the destitute and his observations culminated in the publication of The Road to Wigan Pier – the first book to bring him substantial critical acclaim. The two wars On the cusp of literary success, Orwell decided to travel to Spain, and, like many of his contemporaries – including American writers John Dos Passos and Ernest Hemingway – take part in the bloody Spanish Civil War. His generation of artists and intellectuals followed the events of the Civil War closely, and it became the battleground for political philosophy as much as physical warfare. Orwell’s commitment to fighting fascism in Spain came under scrutiny, as the various factions of the political left were pitted against each other, which left him feeling that the socialist revolution had been betrayed. Returning from the war, he became vocally critical of the Stalinist regime, equating their totalitarianism with that of the fascists across Europe. Left-wing publications that had previously embraced him refused to publish his essays, and his account of the Spanish Civil War, Homage to Catalonia , was refused by his editor Gollancz, eventually going to a smaller publishing house, Secker & Warburg. Having suffered a near-fatal injury in Spain, Orwell’s health continued to deteriorate, and he spent half a year in Morocco recovering, completing his novel Coming Up for Air during his time there. Despite his disillusionment both with his own country’s capitalism and the state of left-wing politics, when the Second World War began Orwell was desperate to fight for his country. This revealed his unique blend of anti-capitalist yet patriotic politics, and his belief that the war could lead to a revolution that united working and middle classes. His thoughts on the topic were explored in his critically acclaimed book, The Lion and the Unicorn . He served in the Home Guard for three years during the war, continued to write numerous essays and reviews for various publications, and later took a job in broadcasting with the BBC, during which time he began his work on Animal Farm .
